turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through. I can see it's been a while — what have you brought me today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the type 2 diabetes. The sugars feel all over the place, and I'm not sleeping for worrying about my feet. People keep saying I'll go blind, and I, um, I can't switch my head off.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. We'll do feet and eyes, but start with the actual treatment. For the type 2 you're on tablets and insulin — talk me through a normal day.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, one gram, twice a day, breakfast and evening meal. Been on that for years. And Lantus at night. I do fourteen units. I think. No — fourteen, I'm sure.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You are not sure, that's the trouble. I was in with him at the diabetes clinic and the nurse said eighteen units of Lantus. She wrote eighteen on the card.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): She said fourteen. Eighteen would flatten me. The card's... I don't know, we didn't bring it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I've got fourteen from you and eighteen from your wife, via the nurse, and no card on the table. I'm not picking a winner yet. Do you actually inject every night?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Most nights. If I'm on an early, out at five, I sometimes skip it. I'm frightened of going low on the bus. Well, not every early. Sometimes.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's work days. Monday to Friday he often doesn't inject at all. I keep finding the pen unused.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That's... alright, maybe three nights a week. I haven't counted. Don't look at me like that.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted, and we'll come back to it, because missed doses change everything else. What are the meter readings? Just read them as they are, even if they're messy.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting this morning was one-eighty-something. Might have been one-eighty-four, the screen jumps. Yesterday was one-eighty-something as well, and I didn't write a single one down.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking aloud here. One-eighty-something in milligrams is around ten millimoles, but something isn't a number I can actually file. What about after food?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): After tea, two hundred and something. Higher. I get shaky if I don't eat, but I haven't actually gone properly low. Is two hundred me ending up in hospital?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two-hundred-and-something milligrams, same idea, is annoying rather than an emergency while you're sitting here talking. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Breathing's been fine.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Eyes. Any blurring, floaters, or a change in what you can see?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Eyes are alright. I had the photograph at the optician last spring, I think, and they said it was fine. I just panic because people talk, that's all.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Feet next. Numbness, tingling, sores, pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine. Honestly. I look at them when I remember, which is not every day.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was up at three rubbing his toes. Go on, tell her. You told me they were on fire.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yes. Both feet, the toes, they burn when I'm in bed. Worse on the right. A few weeks now. If I get up and walk to the loo it eases off.

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Burning in both feet at night, worse on the right, a few weeks, eased by walking. That sounds more like the nerves than an infection, though I'm not stamping a label on it. Any break in the skin, any ulcer?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No sore. No break in the skin. If it's the nerves, does that mean I lose the foot? I need you to say it plainly.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): It does not mean you lose the foot. It means we look, and we sort the sugar. Let me examine them while you're here.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skin is intact on both feet. Pulses are present in both. Monofilament sensation is a bit reduced on the right toes, and normal on the left. There is no ulcer.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Reduced on the right — that's the bad one, isn't it? Should I be on a tablet for the burning? And the metformin, is that quietly damaging my kidneys while we chat?

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Metformin isn't quietly assumed guilty; the kidney bloods will tell us. I was about to reach for a tablet for the burning, but the insulin is the bigger mess. First instinct: put the Lantus up to twenty units every night and see you in a month. On paper that would nudge a fasting sugar in this range downwards.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twenty? The nurse said eighteen and he isn't taking the fourteen. You'll just give him a bigger dose to skip.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want twenty. I'll hypo on the nights I do remember. What if fourteen is actually right and I just take it? Is that stupid?

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, it's sensible, and your wife is right about the skipping. Scratch the increase. I am not changing the insulin dose today. Putting it up while the prescribed dose is disputed and doses are being missed would be unsafe.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what do I do tonight? I need an actual number or I'll lie awake inventing one.

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tonight, stay on the fourteen units you have been drawing up. Do not jump to eighteen because we argued about it, and do not skip it for work. I'll ask the diabetes nurse to confirm the intended dose from the clinic letter.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): If she says eighteen, do I change the same day? And you've gone quiet on the burning tablet. Am I getting one or not?

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You change only when she confirms it, not before. No new tablet for the burning today — I'd rather see if regular insulin settles it. If the burning hasn't eased in a fortnight we might arrange nerve studies, but I am not booking those now.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get a blister before then? Or it suddenly gets worse? Should the eye photo be repeated early? Sorry. I know that's a lot of questions.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blister, sore, or the burning suddenly ramping up — ring the surgery the same day, don't sit on it. The eye screening stays on its normal cycle. You've got no visual symptoms, so I'm not dragging that forward.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Blood tests? And I keep the metformin exactly the same, yes? I keep thinking I should stop it.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the metformin, one gram twice a day, with food, as now. I'll book bloods for straight after this — HbA1c, kidney function, and urine albumin. I nearly sent you back tomorrow fasting, but these don't need to be fasting, so today on the way out is the plan.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll agree in here and then forget on Monday at five. I'm not standing in the kitchen at that hour. I work as well.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): The injection is bedtime, not five in the morning. Set an alarm for when you get into bed. Missing it on work days is doing more damage than the row about four units.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought it had to be the exact same time or it didn't count. That's why I skip, partly. If the shift overruns I just leave it.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same part of the day — night — not the same minute on the clock. If you're late home, do it when you get in. I'm talking this through out loud, so say if I've lost you.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): You haven't. Is the burning definitely the diabetes, though? I did my back years ago, gardening, and it still crosses my mind. Could it just be that?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): It could be diabetic nerve pain, or it could be the old back referring down, and I cannot separate those in this room. That is why I am not labelling it. I'm still not sending you for a back scan. The nerve studies only if this hasn't settled, as I said.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I come back, or do I only ring if it's awful? I don't want to be a nuisance and I also don't want to be left.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are not a nuisance. I'll see you here in six weeks with the blood results, whether the feet have calmed or not — reception will give you the slip. The nerve studies stay a maybe, and only if the burning hasn't eased in a fortnight.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Tonight fourteen, metformin the same, write the numbers down instead of one-eighty-something. What if the meter says something mad, like three hundred, and I feel peculiar?

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the number is very high and you feel unwell — vomiting, drowsy, breathing not right — that is same day, and hospital if you cannot get us. A high number when you feel well goes in the log. Bring the log, and the nurse's card if it turns up, to that six-week visit.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): We will. I have a small whisky at the weekend. Is that finished now as well? I can give it up if you say so. I'd rather know.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): A small whisky at the weekend can stay, as long as you eat and you don't skip the insulin to make room for it. If the card turns up, bring it. Bloods on the way out, fourteen units tonight, and I'll see you in six weeks.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
